Al-Zamakhsharī and others allow it."}, {"id": "11:105/q04/p2", "position": "An implied 'remember' governs it.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī offer this ellipsis."}, {"id": "11:105/q04/p3", "position": "The omitted ending of the fixed term governs it.", "reasons": "The time is when the term in 11:104 reaches its end."}, {"id": "11:105/q04/p4", "position": "An omitted repetition of لا تكلم governs it.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports this fourth proposal but says it is unnecessary."}]}
{"id": "11:105/q05", "question": "How does لا تَكَلَّمُ نَفْسٌ relate syntactically to the Day?", "turns_on": "Which clause relation and ellipsis are adopted.", "positions": [{"id": "11:105/q05/p1", "position": "It begins a new sentence whose fronted time adverb is governed by its verb.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr describes the sentence as resuming the discourse; al-Ṭabrisī prefers direct government."}, {"id": "11:105/q05/p2", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause about the arriving Day.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, Abū ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya supply a pronoun or 'in it'; al-Ḥawfī relates it to the Day of 'witnessed'. Ibn ʿAṭiyya excludes making it a circumstance of the self-annexed phrase."}, {"id": "11:105/q05/p3", "position": "It is an adjective modifying an indefinite يوم.", "reasons": "Indefiniteness follows attachment to a verb; 'in it' is understood. Al-Wāḥidī notes that the adjectival clause can be omitted."}, {"id": "11:105/q05/p4", "position": "It is the predicate of يوم يأتي.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya also allows this analysis."}]}
{"id": "11:105/q06", "question": "Why does تَكَلَّمُ lack a second tāʾ?", "turns_on": "Deletion for ease versus a transmitted assimilated form.", "positions": [{"id": "11:105/q06/p1", "position": "One of the two initial tāʾs of تتكلم is regularly omitted for ease.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash says the weaker second tāʾ is dropped because the sequence is heavy; a connecting hamza cannot replace it in this verb class. Al-Ṭabarī says the surviving tāʾ signals the omitted one; al-Thaʿlabī and al-Ṭabrisī cite analogous forms and poetry. Al-Biqāʿī makes its brevity signify very little speech."}, {"id": "11:105/q06/p2", "position": "A reading assimilates the tāʾ.", "reasons": "Qirāʾāt ER describes idghām with added phonetic gravity and unchanged meaning; al-Nashr lists al-Bazzī's doubling route among future verbs including this verse."}]}
{"id": "11:105/q07", "question": "What speech requires God's permission, and how do the speech passages fit together?", "turns_on": "Whether 'speech' means all utterance, useful defense, good words, a particular station, or compelled disclosure.", "positions": [{"id": "11:105/q07/p1", "position": "No soul may speak at all unless God permits it.", "reasons": "The indefinite soul under negation includes all people and all speech, says Ibn ʿĀshūr; 78:38 and 20:108 are parallels cited by al-Kashshāf, Ibn Kathīr and others. Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports Saʿīd ibn Jubayr's formulation in God's presence; an intercession hadith says only messengers speak, praying for safety. Elmalılı connects permission to the fortunate."}, {"id": "11:105/q07/p2", "position": "Only useful speech, especially defense, accepted proof, or intercession, needs permission.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī prefers intercession or mediation; al-Māwardī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī report versions. Confession, blame and empty argument occur but count as no speech; al-Zajjāj and al-Ṭabrisī compare figurative deafness in 2:18 and 2:171 and cite poetry. Al-Ālūsī prefers saying excuses are not heard or accepted. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that the verse does not restrict speech to another person and that 'no speech' then lacks a coherent permission clause."}, {"id": "11:105/q07/p3", "position": "Only good or truthful answers are permitted, with evil or false excuses barred.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Jubbāʾī say creatures are compelled to leave evil speech; al-Bayḍāwī permits truthful answers. Al-Ālūsī allows false claims when God exposes them. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls the moral restriction unsupported because this is a place of requital and excuses are not sinful acts."}, {"id": "11:105/q07/p4", "position": "The long Resurrection has different stations or moments, some silent and others speaking by permission.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj finds this and the ineffective-speech account both sound; al-Ḥasan and later writers cite 77:35–36, 37:24, 55:39, arguments and bodily testimony. Al-Ālūsī defends differing locations and moments; Elmalılı says one station allows no excuses. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says this still depends on permission and disputes its fit with the verse's scope."}, {"id": "11:105/q07/p5", "position": "Afterlife speech is compelled disclosure, unlike voluntary worldly speech.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says inner states are manifest, records and limbs testify (36:65, 55:39–41), so ordinary sound based disclosure is unnecessary. Speech by permission reveals God's sovereignty already true in this life; lies can arise as ingrained habits but cannot deceive God. He links this to requital without new choice and takes 78:38 as reconciling affirmations and denials; he rejects al-Manār's bare reconciliation."}, {"id": "11:105/q07/p6", "position": "No excuse is requested because there is no duty then and terror forces confession.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this distinct explanation of 77:35–36."}, {"id": "11:105/q07/p7", "position": "The words concern only the first moment when the Day arrives.", "reasons": "A scholar reported by al-Ālūsī confines the statement to that moment."}, {"id": "11:105/q07/p8", "position": "The exception may be disconnected: none speaks by independent power, but God can permit speech.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī offers connected and disconnected analyses; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects the latter as true of every human act in every age."}]}

Ibn ʿĀshūr says this refutes assumed idol intercession."}, {"id": "11:105/q08/p2", "position": "Permission and sole control become manifest on that Day.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says divine permission governs all events always, but the veil lifts then; he compares 40:16, 40:33, 82:19, 50:22, 32:12 and 10:28–30."}]}

{"id": "11:105/q10", "question": "What do شَقِىٌّ and سَعِيدٌ mean in language?", "turns_on": "Whether the terms are described as living conditions, enabling causes, or divine aid.", "positions": [{"id": "11:105/q10/p1", "position": "Wretchedness is hardship and distress; felicity is the contrary ease and pleasant good.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī cites a camel poem for mutual hardship; al-Jishumī defines the strength of causes of harm and blessing; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the adjectives immersion in those states. {"id": "11:105/q12", "question": "Does the twofold division include everyone gathered?", "turns_on": "Whether an apparently exhaustive division is logically exhaustive by wording or by surrounding context.", "positions": [{"id": "11:105/q12/p1", "position": "The context ultimately sends everyone gathered to one of the two outcomes.", "reasons": "Al-Qāḍī argues there is no equal third state or permanent People of the Heights; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says even incapable persons ultimately join a group, comparing 9:106 and 42:7–8. {"id": "11:105/q13", "question": "Are wretchedness and happiness fixed by decree or reached through deeds?", "turns_on": "Whether the inscription describes an unconditional fate, a recompense for action, or an outcome decreed through chosen causes.", "positions": [{"id": "11:105/q13/p1", "position": "They are inscribed by an already settled decree, with each person eased toward the deeds of that end.", "reasons": "ʿUmar's repeated report says pens have run; ʿAlī's funeral report commands work and cites 92:5–10. Al-Rāzī argues a change would falsify God's knowledge, while al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that a future report does not make its state present now."}, {"id": "11:105/q13/p2", "position": "Their own obedient or disobedient deeds are the cause of the outcomes.", "reasons": "Ibn Baḥr calls the states recompense; al-Ḥasan's reported formula says each is wretched or happy by deeds. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī stresses faith and piety versus shirk and sin and cites 53:39–41."}, {"id": "11:105/q13/p3", "position": "God initiates wretchedness or happiness without recompense for deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this second view; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects a deterministic reading that erases genuine choice and action."}, {"id": "11:105/q13/p4", "position": "Decree fixes outcomes through complete causes that include voluntary human action.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes necessity relative to a complete cause from possibility relative to human will, using fire and wood. A truthful forecast does not bring future state into the present; prophetic facilitation presupposes a path and does not make deeds irrelevant. He says 11:105 itself does not settle intrinsic versus acquired status."}, {"id": "11:105/q13/p5", "position": "The decree makes deeds irrelevant, or compels them with no real choice.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī presents these inferred deterministic claims in order to reject them; their premise severs the causal path from deeds to outcome."}]}
{"id": "11:105/q14", "question": "What was reported when the verse raised questions about destiny?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in speaker and subject, while the decree reports share the settled writing and facilitation formula.", "positions": [{"id": "11:105/q14/p1", "position": "ʿUmar asked if deeds concern a settled decree; the Prophet said it was settled and each person is facilitated for their end.", "reasons": "The versions mention dried pens and flowing fates; al-Tirmidhī grades the route ḥasan or ḥasan gharīb. ʿAlī's funeral account adds the command to work and 92:5–10; ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn asks a related question in Bukhārī."}, {"id": "11:105/q14/p2", "position": "A prophetic report says one is wretched or happy from the womb.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd invokes womb status; al-Ālūsī explains the report as an angel learning the decree or disclosure of prior knowledge."}, {"id": "11:105/q14/p3", "position": "The Prophet showed two complete books listing the people of Paradise and Hell.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUmar's account says the books cannot be altered, each end matches deeds, and servants should continue acting."}, {"id": "11:105/q14/p4", "position": "People speak Syriac on Resurrection Day.", "reasons": "Al-Shaʿbī gives this report."}, {"id": "11:105/q14/p5", "position": "Ibn ʿAbbās called the division and the messengers' reply in 5:109 hidden matters.", "reasons": "The notes connect the unseen division to the eventual release of major sinners."}, {"id": "11:105/q14/p6", "position": "Abū Jaʿfar distinguished the exceptions for Hell and Paradise.", "reasons": "Abū Baṣīr reports that the Paradise exception is followed by 'an unsevered gift'."}]}
{"id": "11:105/q15", "question": "Why use these short or indefinite forms and this order?", "turns_on": "Whether brevity, indefiniteness, sequence, or structural division carries the rhetorical point.", "positions": [{"id": "11:105/q15/p1", "position": "Shortened forms evoke nearness, terror, and very little speech.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī reads omitted yāʾ as two thirds of the Day's silence and omitted tāʾ as scant speech; al-Sāmarrāʾī invokes repeated demands for punishment in Hūd, earlier nations' swift downfall, and fewer 'come' derivatives here than in al-Anʿām and al-Aʿrāf."}, {"id": "11:105/q15/p2", "position": "Indefinite singular forms magnify the states and portray each group as a unit.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī takes indefiniteness as exaltation; al-Ālūsī says singularity precedes successive plural entry into the two abodes."}, {"id": "11:105/q15/p3", "position": "The wretched appear first because the surrounding passage warns.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī states the warning explains this order."}, {"id": "11:105/q15/p4", "position": "The division exemplifies warning and a gather, differentiate, divide pattern.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī names warning; al-Itqān and al-Ālūsī say generic soul gathers all, two adjectives separate, and the ensuing أما clauses subdivide, citing al-Sharīf al-Qayrawānī's poem."}]}
{"id": "11:105/q16", "question": "How does this verse connect to its surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "How the gathered assembly, postponed Day, intercession warning and ensuing descriptions fit together.", "positions": [{"id": "11:105/q16/p1", "position": "It explains the witnessed gathering of 11:103 and then introduces the two destinations detailed next.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the opening evokes gravity and the central division resumes after a postponement parenthesis; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes final reckoning from grave questioning; Kuran Yolu links outcomes to worldly faith and deeds."}, {"id": "11:105/q16/p2", "position": "It warns against reliance on intercession.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu reports a context limited to idolaters after stories of idolatrous peoples, but prefers a general warning covering prophets, saints, angels and others; Ibn ʿĀshūr says idols have no right to intercede."}, {"id": "11:105/q16/p3", "position": "The verse's general two groups govern the following أما clauses and exceptions.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects restricting the opening division to selected sinners; he says that leaves repeated subjects, durations and exceptions confusing. {"id": "11:106/q01", "question": "What does it mean that these people became wretched?", "turns_on": "Whether wretchedness names an already decreed destiny, a temporary condition, or an inward orientation.", "positions": [{"id": "11:106/q01/p1", "position": "Their wretchedness was decreed and leads, through their evil deeds, to their being sentenced to Hell.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī says they are called wretched before entering because their present course leads there; his prophetic report about wretchedness in the womb describes foreknown evil deeds, like calling a child an orphan in anticipation. {"id": "11:106/q02", "question": "Who are the wretched destined for the Fire?", "turns_on": "Whether the paired groups include everyone gathered, and whether wretchedness describes temporary punishment or only final destiny.", "positions": [{"id": "11:106/q02/p1", "position": "All who are punished in Hell, including unbelievers and sinful believers.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya ties the scope to the following exception; al-Jishumī says sinners are included against the Murjiʾa. {"id": "11:106/q09", "question": "What inward meaning is drawn from the two sounds?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:106/q09/p1", "position": "Zafīr evokes strong attachment to worldly pleasures; shahīq evokes inability to reach spiritual bliss and divine lights.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī offers this spiritual reading alongside his lexical accounts."}]}
{"id": "11:106/q10", "question": "How does the sounds clause attach grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause stands as a new predication or describes a circumstance of their being in Hell.", "positions": [{"id": "11:106/q10/p1", "position": "It is a separate sentence answering an implied question about their condition.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī present this analysis; al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī also treat it as continued predication."}, {"id": "11:106/q10/p2", "position": "It is circumstantial, linked to the implicit existential in 'in the Fire,' its pronoun, or the Fire itself.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī identifies the implicit existential; al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī give the pronoun or Fire as possible anchors."}]}
{"id": "11:106/q11", "question": "Why are zafīr and shahīq left indefinite and singled out?", "turns_on": "Whether the wording emphasizes the ghastliness of the sounds or their warning effect.", "positions": [{"id": "11:106/q11/p1", "position": "The indefinite nouns magnify the unprecedented horror of their gasps and sobs.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says the forms intensify the scene; al-Qāshānī says, alternatively, indefiniteness may indicate kinds of sounds."}, {"id": "11:106/q11/p2", "position": "Naming their disfiguring breaths makes the warning more frightening than simply naming pain.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the sounds deter people from the causes of damnation; Bursevī compares them to ugly cries and bodily changes in worldly torture, with the afterlife worse."}]}

{"id": "11:108/q01", "question": "How does the division introduced by وَأَمَّا present the two groups and their fates?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:108/q01/p1", "position": "It elaborates the gathering by dividing all souls into the wretched and fortunate, then setting out their destinations.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says the final judgment strengthens the Prophet for his mission; al-Ālūsī cites the successive fa particles and al-Sharīf al-Qayrawānī’s poem for the gathering-to-classification pattern; Kuranyolu links 11:103 and worldly faith and deeds."}, {"id": "11:108/q01/p2", "position": "The division also signals that felicity and misery were settled beforehand.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī infers this from the sequence of fa particles."}]}
{"id": "11:108/q02", "question": "Who are ٱلَّذِينَ سُعِدُوا۟?", "turns_on": "Whether the label names all believers by their final destiny, those transferred from Hell, or graded states of happiness.", "positions": [{"id": "11:108/q02/p1", "position": "They are the faithful and obedient, especially followers of the messengers, who receive Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī names obedience and avoidance of sin; Ibn Kathīr names followers of the messengers; Elmalılı contrasts believers who humble themselves with seekers of worldly life in 11:15–16, 23; Kuranyolu ties destiny to faith and deeds."}, {"id": "11:108/q02/p2", "position": "They include monotheists who first suffer in Hell and later become fortunate in Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk via Ibn ʿAbbās says they become happy after earlier misery; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī explains that the same persons can be wretched in Hell and happy in Paradise; his objection is that the verse's two groups are exhaustive, so neither can be reduced to former sinners alone."}, {"id": "11:108/q02/p3", "position": "The happy have ranks: some remain within Paradise's grades, while the happier ascend to divine proximity.", "reasons": "Bursevī's Najmiyya account grounds the higher stations in knowledge, piety, and love, citing 54:54–55; a hadith likens the people of ʿIlliyyīn to bright stars and names Abū Bakr and ʿUmar."}]}
{"id": "11:108/q03", "question": "What does سُعِدُوا۟ mean?", "turns_on": "Active saʿidū versus passive suʿidū affects whether divine causation is overt.", "positions": [{"id": "11:108/q03/p1", "position": "The passive expression says they were granted or made happy by God.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī notes passive majnūn and maḥbūb; al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, and al-Bayḍāwī give this meaning; al-Ālūsī sees a call to gratitude, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī contrasts God-given good with self-caused evil in 24:21."}, {"id": "11:108/q03/p2", "position": "It denotes felicity, the opposite of wretchedness, with success and ease.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī gives saʿāda, saʿd, saʿīd; al-Ṭabrisī contrasts shaqāʾ and traces the yāʾ of shaqī to wāw; al-Jawharī compares salima; al-Biqāʿī glosses attaining aims and ease."}]}

{"id": "11:108/q07", "question": "What are the ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتُ وَٱلْأَرْضُ whose duration is mentioned?", "turns_on": "Whether the wording is idiom, refers to transformed afterlife creation, or measures a worldly term; objections concern literal perishability, audience familiarity, and the plural heavens.", "positions": [{"id": "11:108/q07/p1", "position": "The phrase is a familiar Arabic idiom for indefinite or everlasting duration.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba lists night and day, rising seas, mountains, heaven and earth; al-Ṭabrisī cites ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib and Zuhayr; al-Kashshāf cites Taʿār, Thabīr and stars. {"id": "11:108/q08", "question": "How is مَا دَامَتِ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتُ وَٱلْأَرْضُ parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the duration is treated as conventional perpetuity or analyzed as a condition whose converse does not follow.", "positions": [{"id": "11:108/q08/p1", "position": "Mā forms a temporal verbal noun: for the duration that the heavens and earth remain; dāma is complete.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, Bursevī and al-Burhān explain this temporal maṣdariyya; al-Burhān contrasts non-temporal mā and distinguishes relative mā elsewhere."}, {"id": "11:108/q08/p2", "position": "The phrase measures an immense span without logically proving what follows if that condition ends.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reasons that denying the condition does not deny its consequent, just as a nonhuman can still be an animal; he also answers a critic of the idiom argument."}]}
